Today I tweaked WhoaVerse database in order to "get more juice" out of available resources so I hope you guys will notice a more responsive WhoaVerse. There are plenty of other things that need to be done in order to get the best possible performance so I'll keep experimenting until we get there :) If you do notice a weird query in one of the controllers, please feel free to comment or submit a pull request.

A few rules of thumb from my database performance tuning professor:

  • avoid the use of distinct and cartesian product
  • use clustering indexes for joins
  • avoid using subqueries
  • do not use unnecessary joins
I'd add just make sure Foreign Keys have non-clustered indexes on them for join purposes.

Oddly enough, my professor stated today that clustering indexes should be used for join purposes. Google search returns a weird set of results on this subject, nothing conclusive. I guess we should test and see what works best.

You want clustered on the PK, and non-clustered on all FK's if you want fast reads. More indexes = more insertion overhead though. I think your prof might not be explaining clearly because you can't have more than 1 clustered index on a table and that is usually the PK, so thus non-clustered have to be used on FK columns so the join can navigate indexes rather than leaf level data.

More of a personal thing:

DON'T USE GUID's FOR PKs, PLEASE! I BEG OF YOU.

I second this 100 times. I've had this discussion with several people at various jobs.

Relevant post with stats

TL;DR: It's not just a 'personal thing'. Using GUIDs for indexing large tables causes very poor performance in update/insert and join/sort operations

I said personal because I think you would have to be full-retard to index GUIDs and have Foreign Keys on them BUT... You can force sequentially incremented GUIDs which won't trash a clustered index. Don't tell anyone about this ever because once they learn this they think everything would be fine then.

Personally, I think GUIDs make it very hard for Humans to read and interpret data. I'd rather look up a record with ID = 4544 rather than ID = '7A344592-CE78-46A7-A8AB-27099E8F9E68'
